consensus_summary: Wheat primarily symbolizes the righteous or true believers—the 'children of the kingdom'—gathered by God at the eschatological harvest, contrasted with tares/chaff destined for judgment. Anchored in Matthew 13:24-30, 36-43 and Matthew 3:12/Luke 3:17. Common secondary senses include Christ's death and resurrection (John 12:24), divine provision/blessing, and Eucharistic bread.
book_summary: Wheat is the children of the kingdom—the good grain gathered into the barn at the harvest—explicitly set opposite to tares. Cites Matthew 13:38 and Matthew 3:12.
consensus_core_identification: The genuine people of God / true believers (children of the kingdom) gathered at the final harvest, distinguished from the wicked (tares/chaff).
book_core_identification: The children of the kingdom, the good grain gathered into the barn at the harvest, opposite of tares.
boundary_disagreement: None. The book's entry is a concise restatement of the consensus primary identification, including the same harvest/barn imagery and the same contrast with tares. It omits secondary senses (John 12:24 death-and-fruit, provision, Eucharist), but omission of alternatives in a glossary entry does not constitute a boundary change to the core identification.
rationale: All four consensus responses identify wheat's primary meaning as the righteous/true believers gathered at God's eschatological harvest, based chiefly on Matthew 13 and Matthew 3:12. The book entry says exactly this—'children of the kingdom, the good grain gathered into the barn at the harvest,' opposite tares—citing the same two proof texts. The wording 'children of the kingdom' is directly drawn from Matthew 13:38, which the consensus responses also quote. There is no narrowing, broadening, or replacement of referent.
strongest_objection: The book entry ignores the well-attested secondary uses of wheat imagery (Christ's death in John 12:24, divine provision, Eucharistic bread), so one could argue it presents a narrower total account than the consensus. However, the consensus itself treats those as distinct contextual uses rather than rivals to the primary meaning, so this omission does not alter the core identification.
